name: Heavy compound lifting for testosterone

lead: Heavy squats, deadlifts and other big barbell lifts build muscle directly, and lifters also do them for the testosterone rise that follows, aiming for a more muscular, masculine look.

Large multi-joint lifts engage a lot of muscle and produce acute hormone responses, including testosterone, growth hormone and catecholamines, around the session. Reference texts confirm short-term testosterone rises after resistance exercise, with squats in particular producing acute increases in men; whether this changes resting levels over time is not shown in the sources reviewed.

paras: People build programs around a few heavy compound lifts several times a week, adding weight progressively and pairing training with enough food and sleep. Visible muscle changes typically take months.
Lifting carries the usual training-related injury risks, such as back and joint strain, which technique and gradual progression help reduce. No hormonal harms are described in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Heavy squats and deadlifts build muscle directly and raise testosterone for a while after each session, for a more masculine physique. Lasting changes in baseline testosterone are not established in the sources reviewed.

lead: Heavy compound lifting for testosterone is the practice of building training around large multi-joint barbell exercises such as squats and deadlifts in the belief that they raise testosterone, which proponents link to more muscle, leaner body composition and a more masculine physique. Setting the hormone effect aside, the lifts load large amounts of muscle, which is the direct route to a fuller, more muscular look.[1]

Reference texts report that resistance training raises testosterone acutely, meaning a temporary rise around the session, and that squats in particular produce acute increases in men.[2][1] A 2026 PeerJ systematic review of randomized trials reported that testosterone rose more after resistance training than after aerobic exercise and took longer to return to baseline, with aerobic exercise values typically recovering within about an hour.[3]

Reviewers also describe wide variability in results, attributing it to exercise type, intensity and rest periods, who is studied (age, body fat, fitness) and when blood is sampled.[4] A 2020 narrative review concluded that exercise does not seem to increase resting testosterone in healthy men, and found no solid evidence that the acute spike improves muscle growth.[4] The research describes short-term hormone changes; no trial located tests whether heavy compound lifting durably raises resting testosterone.

paras: Compound lifts recruit several large muscle groups at once. In the squat, the primary movers include the quadriceps, gluteus maximus, adductor magnus and soleus, with the erector spinae, abdominals, obliques and hamstrings acting as stabilizers; Wikipedia describes it as a large muscle-mass resistance exercise and a vital exercise for increasing lower-body strength and size.[1] Proponents favour such lifts for testosterone because they involve a large amount of muscle mass, and a 2020 review found that small-muscle work did not raise testosterone above rest while multi-joint, large-muscle exercise did.[4]

Wikipedia's testosterone article states that resistance training raises testosterone acutely, that in older men protein intake may blunt that rise, and that endurance training in men may lead to lower testosterone.[2] The squat article reports acute increases in testosterone in men, in growth hormone more in women, and in catecholamines, and notes that resistance-trained people have higher resting IGF-1.[1]

A 2020 review by Riachy and colleagues found that resistance exercise produced larger acute rises than endurance exercise and that resistance-trained men showed the biggest increases. In one study, a session of four sets of 10 squats at 75 percent of one-repetition maximum with 90-second rests raised testosterone, with the elevation persisting for 48 hours; free-weight squats produced a larger rise than Smith machine or leg press work, which the authors linked to greater stabilizer and core involvement. Older and middle-aged men still rose acutely but usually by less, and obese men showed blunted responses in several studies.[4] The review reported that acute rises after resistance exercise usually return to baseline, or dip below it, within about 30 minutes.[4]

The same review concluded that exercise does not seem to increase resting testosterone in healthy men, that long-term endurance training lowered resting levels in some studies, and that evidence in older men is conflicting; in obese men some programmes raised resting testosterone but coincided with fat loss, so the cause was unclear. It also reported no solid evidence that the acute spike improves muscle hypertrophy.[4]
Wikipedia's article lists other lifestyle factors associated with testosterone, including age, weight loss, sleep, vitamin D and zinc status, without attributing resting-level change to lifting.[2]

Human studies have measured testosterone around single sessions of resistance exercise. A 2026 PeerJ systematic review followed PRISMA and searched five databases through March 2025; its abstract reports 15 randomized trials with 251 participants, while its results section reports 16 trials with 267 participants, and the synthesis was qualitative. Ten trials reported a significant post-exercise increase, five found no significant change and one found a decrease.[3]

The review reported larger testosterone rises after resistance training than aerobic exercise, with aerobic values typically back to baseline within about an hour, and said prolonged high-intensity exercise was linked to suppression during recovery that could last up to 72 hours. Males had higher baselines and stronger responses than females, responses were greater in younger males than older adults and negligible in adolescents, and the authors noted small samples, heterogeneous protocols and mostly moderate risk of bias.[3] A 2020 review described the response as varying with exercise type, intensity, population and sampling time.[4] No trial located tests whether heavy compound lifting raises resting testosterone over months or years.

T Nation forum members discuss the hormonal release triggered by different lifts and loads alongside local muscle stimulation as factors in muscle growth.[5] Discussions on the same forum of low testosterone and hormone therapy often raise training, diet and lifestyle as contributors, with one poster describing poor diet and training as capable of inducing hypogonadism.[6]

lore.intro: In lifting forums, heavy compound movements are often discussed as having a hormonal benefit in addition to their muscle-building effect.[5]

claims.claim: Heavy squats and deadlifts boost testosterone and so build more muscle.
Lifting heavy can raise baseline testosterone long term.
Free-weight squats raise testosterone more than machine alternatives.
